newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany to require warnings for passenger airbags.
newsitem.headline: Germany to require warnings for passenger airbags.

text.p: Germany said on Wednesday it plans to require car makers to include a label on the passenger-side dashboard warning against the risks to small children from the sudden inflation of air bags during an accident.

Transport Minister Matthias Wissmann told reporters that a government regulation would take effect later this year that aimed to warn parents against transporting infants and toddlers in infant safety seats in front of air bags.
While airbags are credited with saving hundreds of lives over the years, at least 30 children have also been killed by the rapid inflation of the bags -- at up to 200 miles an hour (320 kph).
Experts say small adults and frail older people are also at risk.

Safety advocates in the United States have urged the use of so-called dual-inflation airbags that inflate more slowly in low-speed crashes, which cause only minor or moderate injuries, but faster in life-threatening high speed crashes.
They also want manufacturers to include an off-switch to be able to deactivate the airbag mechanism.

The U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration in 1991 warned parents that children in infant safety seats should not be placed in front of an airbag and in 1995 the agency publicly stated that airbags could cause injuries and death.
The German regulation is intended to urge parents to place children on the rear seat and to use safety belts and an infant safety seat.
Government data show that fewer than half of all children transported in cars wear safety belts in downtown traffic and on rural highways just 40 percent, the transport minister said.
